meta.title: Multiplying Polynomials
meta.description: Master tabular area multiplication (box method) and prove closure under polynomial multiplication.
meta.pageDescription: Explore tabular box method, FOIL method generalizations, degree properties, and polynomial multiplication closure.
meta.author: Hesten's Learning Team

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 9
overview.text: In this lesson, you will extend the distributive property to multiply any two polynomials. Using tabular area grids (the box method), you will organize partial products systematically, combine diagonal like terms, and verify that the product of polynomials is always a polynomial.
outcomes: Understand that the product of two polynomials is always another polynomial (closure under multiplication).
Multiply binomials and trinomials using the tabular box method and generalized distributive property.
Understand that the degree of the product of two non-zero polynomials is the sum of their individual degrees: $\deg(P \cdot Q) = \deg(P) + \deg(Q)$.
overview.teacherInsight: The tabular area model prevents missing terms in higher-degree multiplications like $(x^2 + 2x - 1)(x^3 - 4x + 2)$. Remind students to check the diagonal diagonals in the box to easily spot like terms.

vocabulary.definition: A polynomial with exactly two terms, such as x + 4 or 3x² - 2.
A polynomial with exactly three terms, such as ax² + bx + c.
A geometric organizer where terms of one polynomial form rows and terms of the other form columns, computing all partial products systematically.
For non-zero polynomials P and Q, deg(P · Q) = deg(P) + deg(Q).

practiceQuestions.question: What is the product of $(w^2 + 1)(w^3 - w + 1)$ in standard form?
If polynomial $P(x)$ has degree 3 and polynomial $Q(x)$ has degree 4, what is the degree of $P(x) \cdot Q(x)$?
practiceQuestions.explanation: When multiplying polynomials, exponents of leading terms add together: $x^3 \cdot x^4 = x^{3+4} = x^7$. The degree of the product is 3 + 4 = 7.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Multiplying a Trinomial by a Binomial (The Tabular Method)
guidedExercises.problem: Multiply $(2x - 3)(3x^2 - 4x + 5)$ and write the product as a polynomial in standard form.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Set up a $2 \times 3$ grid or distribute $2x$ and $-3$ across each term of the trinomial. Be careful with signs and exponent addition.

steps.label: Align and combine like terms
steps.explanation: Sum the quadratic terms ($-8 - 9 = -17$) and linear terms ($10 + 12 = 22$).

guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Omitting the middle terms when squaring binomials: $(a + b)^2 \neq a^2 + b^2$. The correct expansion is $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$. For example, $(x + 4)^2 = x^2 + 8x + 16$, NOT $x^2 + 16$!

guidedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Expanding Binomial Products with Difference of Squares
guidedExercises.problem: Multiply $(3x - 5)(3x + 5)$ and $(2x + 7)^2$. Compare how conjugate pairs eliminate linear middle terms.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Conjugates $(a - b)(a + b)$ produce $a^2 - b^2$. Perfect squares $(a + b)^2$ produce $a^2 + 2ab + b^2$.

steps.label: Expand conjugate pair $(3x - 5)(3x + 5)$
steps.explanation: The linear terms $+15x$ and $-15x$ sum to zero (Difference of Squares).

guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Assuming $(3x)^2 = 3x^2$. When squaring a monomial with a coefficient, square both the coefficient and the variable: $(3x)^2 = 3^2 x^2 = 9x^2$.
